title: A Room With No Way Out

scenes.tts: Why can one missing enzyme kill a child, when her parents, with half as much, are fine? The answer is a room with no way out.
scenes.visual: COLOR MAP for the whole film (state it in a comment atop scenes.py): BLUE = membrane (every wall and the lysosome's skin), GOLD = GM2 (and gangliosides generally, as small gold lozenges), TEAL = HexA (a small pair-of-jaws shape that closes), GREEN = delivery (the tap and incoming vesicles), PURPLE = small parts and the transporter door, RED = trouble (high storage, empty enzyme bars), WHITE = oxygen, PALE YELLOW = oily membrane core, PINK = acidic interior. Labels size 30 or larger, full opacity, at most 5 words, at most 6 things on screen. No molecular structures anywhere: blobs, lozenges, bars, cartoons, computed curves. NO title card first and no fade from black. Open on three simple cartoon figures standing side by side filling about 65% of the frame height: two adults (left, centre) and a smaller child (right), plain rounded silhouettes in TEXT outline. Each figure has a vertical bar gauge beside it labelled 'HexA'. They breathe (a slow 2% scale bob by updater) the whole scene. On 'one missing enzyme' the child's bar drains to empty and its outline turns RED. On 'her parents' the two adult bars fill to exactly the half mark, TEAL, with a chip 'half' (TEAL, 30) on each; the adults stay in TEXT outline. On 'are fine' a small GREEN tick appears above each adult. On 'a room with no way out' the three figures slide left and shrink to 30% height; in the freed right two-thirds a BLUE circle draws itself (radius about 2.6), with eight GOLD lozenges drifting inside it and bumping off the wall (updater; none ever crosses), and a GOLD '?' badge (40) pops at its upper right.
scenes.narration: Why can one missing enzyme kill a child, when her parents, with half as much, are fine? The answer is a room with no way out.

scenes.visual: Do not cut away: the BLUE circle with its drifting GOLD lozenges stays at 25% opacity, still moving. Over it: BIOCHEMISTRYPEDIA (TEAL), the title 'A Room With No Way Out' (TITLE_FONT 54) and a GOLD rule. Title out in the last 0.4 s. The circle opens back out into a straight horizontal band during that fade, ready for s02.

scenes.tts: Start with a wall. A cell membrane is a double layer of lipids with an oily core. Small nonpolar molecules, like oxygen, slip straight through. Glucose and ions need doors the cell builds.
scenes.visual: THE WALL: a thick horizontal BLUE band across the full frame width (x -6..6), about 1.6 units tall, at y 0, drawn as two rows of small BLUE head-dots with a pale-yellow core stripe between them (schematic). Above the band 'outside', below it 'inside' (TEXT 28). On 'double layer' the two rows of dots pulse in turn, top row then bottom row. On 'oily core' the stripe brightens and its label 'oily core' (TEXT 28) appears. On 'like oxygen' four small WHITE dots with a chip 'oxygen' (TEXT 30) drift down from the top and pass straight through the band without slowing, then keep drifting back and forth across it (updater) for the rest of the scene. On 'Glucose and ions' a chip 'glucose' and two small chips 'K+' (TEXT 30) fall onto the top of the band and bounce back up, bounce once more, and then on 'doors the cell builds' two PURPLE door shapes open in the band (one channel, one carrier, together labelled 'doors', PURPLE 30); the glucose and K+ chips slide down through them to the inside.
scenes.narration: Start with a wall. A cell membrane is a double layer of lipids with an oily core. Small nonpolar molecules, like oxygen, slip straight through. Glucose and ions need doors the cell builds.

scenes.tts: Close that wall into a bag, and you have a room. The lysosome is the cell's recycling room, with digestive enzymes sealed inside, in acid. Old membrane is delivered in. The enzymes cut it into small parts, which leave through transporters.
scenes.visual: The oxygen dots, glucose and K+ chips fade. On 'into a bag' the BLUE band bends up at both ends and closes into a large BLUE round outline that fills about 70% of the frame height (centre x -1), labelled 'lysosome' (BLUE 30). THIS IS THE CARRIED WORLD for the rest of the film: keep it in the same place. On 'recycling room' the lysosome settles at full size. On 'digestive enzymes' six TEAL jaw-shapes appear inside, slowly opening and closing (updater). On 'in acid' the lysosome's interior tints faintly pink and a chip 'acidic' (TEXT 30) settles at its top edge. On 'delivered in' a GREEN vesicle (small circle carrying three mixed TEXT-outline chips) glides in from the upper left, touches the lysosome and merges with it (its outline becomes part of the BLUE wall), dropping its chips inside; a GREEN label 'delivery in' (30) sits by the entry point, and a second vesicle follows a few seconds later. On 'small parts' each TEAL jaw closes on a chip and the chip splits into three small PURPLE dots. The 'acidic' chip and delivery label fade. On 'leave through transporters' a PURPLE door in the lower-right wall opens and the PURPLE dots stream out through it (continuous trickle by updater), labelled 'transporter' (PURPLE 30).
scenes.narration: Close that wall into a bag, and you have a room. The lysosome is the cell's recycling room, with digestive enzymes sealed inside, in acid. Old membrane is delivered in. The enzymes cut it into small parts, which leave through transporters.

scenes.tts: Now follow one lipid in that old membrane, G M two ganglioside. One enzyme, Hex A, snips one sugar off it, so its breakdown can go on. G M two's big sugar head cannot cross the lysosome's membrane. And no transporter carries it out.
scenes.caption: Now follow one lipid in that old membrane, GM2 ganglioside. One enzyme, HexA, snips one sugar off it, so its breakdown can go on. GM2's big sugar head cannot cross the lysosome's membrane. And no transporter carries it out.
scenes.visual: Same world. On 'follow one lipid' the other cargo fades and the next GREEN vesicle brings in short internal membrane strips carrying GOLD lozenges, each embedded by one end with a fat rounded GOLD knob exposed (the 'sugar head', schematic, no structure), labelled 'GM2' (GOLD 32). GM2 stays membrane-bound throughout this physical view. On 'One enzyme' five of the TEAL jaws dim to 50% and one jaw grows slightly and is labelled 'HexA' (TEAL 32). On 'snips one sugar' it closes on an exposed GOLD knob; the knob's tip pops off as a PURPLE dot and the rest moves on to a TEXT-outline jaw labelled 'next enzymes' (TEXT 28), which breaks it into PURPLE dots that leave by the transporter. On 'cannot cross' one membrane-bound GOLD lozenge approaches the BLUE wall, pushes on it, and bounces back (the wall flexes slightly). On 'no transporter carries' the same membrane-bound lozenge approaches the PURPLE door, which stays closed to it, and it bounces back again.
scenes.narration: Now follow one lipid in that old membrane, GM2 ganglioside. One enzyme, HexA, snips one sugar off it, so its breakdown can go on. GM2's big sugar head cannot cross the lysosome's membrane. And no transporter carries it out.

scenes.tts: Nothing else in the cell does Hex A's job well enough to stand in. So, in its simplest form, this room is a tap and a drain. What it holds is set by delivery in, against clearance out.
scenes.caption: Nothing else in the cell does HexA's job well enough to stand in. So, in its simplest form, this room is a tap and a drain. What it holds is set by delivery in, against clearance out.
scenes.visual: Same lysosome. On 'Nothing else' the five dimmed TEAL jaws each try a GOLD lozenge and fail (they snap shut beside it); only the HexA jaw cuts. On 'tap and a drain' the physical membrane strips transform into a schematic: free GOLD lozenges now represent units of GM2, not literal free-floating molecules. The picture gains two handles, drawn on the lysosome itself: a GREEN tap above the upper-left wall, from which GOLD lozenges drip in at a steady rate, labelled 'delivery in' (GREEN 30); and a TEAL drain at the bottom, a funnel whose mouth width stands for the amount of HexA, labelled 'clearance: HexA' (TEAL 30). GOLD lozenges that reach the drain turn into PURPLE dots and leave. A vertical level gauge appears at the right edge of the frame, labelled 'GM2 in the room' (GOLD 30), its GOLD fill sitting low and steady (schematic). On 'delivery in, against clearance out' the tap and drain pulse in turn (GREEN, then TEAL) and the gauge fill wobbles slightly around its low steady level.
scenes.narration: Nothing else in the cell does HexA's job well enough to stand in. So, in its simplest form, this room is a tap and a drain. What it holds is set by delivery in, against clearance out.

scenes.tts: Each parent has one working copy of the gene. Each makes about half the normal amount of Hex A. So halve the drain. Does their lysosome fill up?
scenes.caption: Each parent has one working copy of the gene. Each makes about half the normal amount of HexA. So halve the drain. Does their lysosome fill up?
scenes.visual: Same world: tap dripping, lysosome, drain, gauge. On 'one working copy' a small adult cartoon from s00 appears in the top-left corner with two gene chips beside it: one 'HEXA' chip TEAL (working), one 'HEXA' chip RED with a cross (broken) (30). On 'half the normal amount' the HexA jaw count inside drops from six to three, and the TEAL drain funnel's mouth narrows to exactly half its width (animated squeeze). On 'Does their lysosome fill up' a question card slides up in the lower third: 'Half drain—does it fill?' (TEXT 36), while the tap keeps dripping and the gauge holds at its old level.
scenes.narration: Each parent has one working copy of the gene. Each makes about half the normal amount of HexA. So halve the drain. Does their lysosome fill up?

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause. The question card 'Half drain—does it fill?' stays on screen at full opacity. The GOLD lozenges keep dripping from the tap and drifting in the lysosome; the gauge does not move yet. Nothing else changes.

scenes.tts: No. A normal lysosome has far more Hex A than it needs. It clears G M two many times faster than it arrives. Halve the drain, and the level settles a little higher, but stays low.
scenes.caption: No. A normal lysosome has far more HexA than it needs. It clears GM2 many times faster than it arrives. Halve the drain, and the level settles a little higher, but stays low.
scenes.visual: On 'No' the question card slides away. The lysosome shrinks to the left half of the frame (tap, half drain and gauge come with it). In the right half a PLOT draws in: x axis 'time', y axis 'GM2 in the room' (TEXT 28), with a tag 'toy model, illustrative' (TEXT 28) at its corner. The curves are COMPUTED from the lesson's toy model (Going deeper, 'The balance in numbers'): dS/dt = k_in - f*S/(1+S), with k_in = 0.1 (delivery is a tenth of what normal HexA clears at full speed), S in units of Km, f = HexA fraction of normal, S(0) = 0. On 'far more Hex A' the f = 1.0 curve (TEAL, labelled 'normal') draws left to right and flattens at S = 0.11. On 'many times faster' a short GREEN arrow (delivery) and a TEAL arrow ten times as long (top clearing speed) appear side by side under the plot. The arrows fade before the next curve draws. On 'Halve the drain' the f = 0.5 curve (TEAL dashed, labelled 'half: carrier') draws and flattens at S = 0.25, about twice the normal level; in the lysosome the gauge fill rises a little and settles. On 'stays low' a RED dashed line labelled 'high storage, schematic' (RED 28) sits high on the plot (S = 1.5), far above both curves, and the GREEN tick from s00 pops beside the carrier curve.
scenes.narration: No. A normal lysosome has far more HexA than it needs. It clears GM2 many times faster than it arrives. Halve the drain, and the level settles a little higher, but stays low.

scenes.tts: In the infantile form, there is almost no working enzyme. The drain is almost shut, but delivery goes on, from before birth. G M two piles up, and the lysosomes swell. Yet the room stays intact, filling with something it cannot empty.
scenes.caption: In the infantile form, there is almost no working enzyme. The drain is almost shut, but delivery goes on, from before birth. GM2 piles up, and the lysosomes swell. Yet the room stays intact, filling with something it cannot empty.
scenes.visual: On 'almost no working enzyme' the small cartoon in the corner becomes the child from s00 with two RED crossed 'HEXA' chips; the remaining TEAL jaws in the lysosome fade out and the drain funnel squeezes nearly closed (a thin TEAL slit). On 'delivery goes on' the GREEN tap keeps dripping at exactly the same rate as before. In the plot, the f = 0 curve (RED, labelled 'zero: toy model') draws as a straight line rising at slope 0.1, crossing the 'high storage, schematic' line and leaving the top of the plot; the axes do not rescale. On 'piles up' GOLD lozenges stack in concentric layers inside the lysosome and the gauge fill climbs steadily (it keeps climbing to the end of the scene). On 'lysosomes swell' the BLUE outline grows by about 30%, stretching but staying one smooth unbroken line. On 'stays intact' the BLUE wall flashes once, still one unbroken line; no GOLD ever leaves.
scenes.narration: In the infantile form, there is almost no working enzyme. The drain is almost shut, but delivery goes on, from before birth. GM2 piles up, and the lysosomes swell. Yet the room stays intact, filling with something it cannot empty.

scenes.tts: Storage starts only when the drain falls below the tap. Measurements put that cut-off near ten to fifteen percent of normal, far below half. Below it, leftover enzyme slows the rise, so the illness starts later.
scenes.caption: Storage starts only when the drain falls below the tap. Measurements put that cut-off near 10 to 15% of normal, far below half. Below it, leftover enzyme slows the rise, so the illness starts later.
scenes.visual: The swollen lysosome eases back to its carrier size, drain at half width again, on the left; the plot stays on the right with its zero-activity curve and its 'toy model, illustrative' tag, while the normal and carrier curves fade. On 'drain falls below the tap' a horizontal dial appears under the plot running from 0 to 1 (normal), labelled 'HexA left' (TEAL 30), with a knob that slides slowly leftwards from 0.5; the drain in the lysosome narrows in step with the knob. As the knob passes 0.2 the f = 0.2 curve (TEAL dotted, labelled '0.2') draws in and flattens at S = 1.0, about nine times normal; as it reaches 0.1 the f = 0.1 curve (thin TEAL, labelled '0.1') draws in and keeps rising without flattening (both computed from the same toy model). On 'ten to fifteen percent' a RED band on the dial covers 0.10 to 0.15, labelled 'measured cut-off' (RED 28). On 'far below half' a TEAL bracket spans the dial from 0.15 to 0.5, labelled 'still keeps up' (TEAL 28). The band and bracket fade. On 'slows the rise' the 0.1 and zero-activity curves are highlighted together so the slower climb of 0.1 against the steeper zero-activity line is clear, and a chip 'later onset' (TEXT 30) appears beside the 0.1 curve.
scenes.narration: Storage starts only when the drain falls below the tap. Measurements put that cut-off near 10 to 15% of normal, far below half. Below it, leftover enzyme slows the rise, so the illness starts later.

scenes.tts: Why are nerve cells hit hardest? Their membranes are rich in gangliosides, so delivery is high. And neurons do not divide. A dividing cell splits its stored G M two between its daughters. A neuron cannot dilute stored G M two that way.
scenes.caption: Why are nerve cells hit hardest? Their membranes are rich in gangliosides, so delivery is high. And neurons do not divide. A dividing cell splits its stored GM2 between its daughters. A neuron cannot dilute stored GM2 that way.
scenes.visual: The plot and dial slide off. The frame splits into two panels filling the height: LEFT a round cell labelled 'dividing cell' (TEXT 30), RIGHT a neuron cartoon labelled 'neuron' (TEXT 30), each holding one small BLUE lysosome with a GREEN tap and a nearly shut TEAL drain (both lack HexA). On 'rich in gangliosides' the neuron's tap opens wider and drips GOLD faster than the dividing cell's tap, with a GREEN chip 'high delivery' (30). On 'do not divide' a RED chip 'no division' (28) appears on the neuron. On 'splits its stored' the left cell pinches into two daughters and its GOLD stack splits evenly between them, each daughter's level dropping to half; both daughters then refill slowly. On 'cannot dilute' the neuron's GOLD stack keeps climbing steadily, never dropping, to the end of the scene.
scenes.narration: Why are nerve cells hit hardest? Their membranes are rich in gangliosides, so delivery is high. And neurons do not divide. A dividing cell splits its stored GM2 between its daughters. A neuron cannot dilute stored GM2 that way.

scenes.tts: So a sealed room keeps whatever reaches it and is not cleared. Half a drain still keeps up, so the parents are fine. With almost no drain, the room fills, and nerve cells are hit hardest.
scenes.visual: Return to the opening world: the three cartoon figures from s00 come back across the bottom third (adults with half-filled TEAL HexA bars and GREEN ticks, child with an almost-empty RED bar). Above each figure a small lysosome with tap and drain: the adults' drains half width with a low steady GOLD level; the child's drain nearly shut and its GOLD level rising. On 'sealed room' all three lysosome outlines pulse BLUE. On 'still keeps up' the two adult lysosomes' levels wobble and settle low. On 'almost no drain' the child's lysosome fills and swells, its outline unbroken, and on 'hit hardest' a small neuron icon beside it glows GOLD. Taps keep dripping throughout.
scenes.narration: So a sealed room keeps whatever reaches it and is not cleared. Half a drain still keeps up, so the parents are fine. With almost no drain, the room fills, and nerve cells are hit hardest.

scenes.visual: End card over the living tap-and-drain lysosome at 20% opacity (lozenges still dripping in and leaving by the drain). LINE (TITLE_FONT 40): 'What a room holds: delivery in, against clearance out.' Below it: biochemistrypedia.com (TEAL).
